prompt: Why does Godot use composition (combining nodes) rather than inheritance (deep class hierarchies) as its primary architecture?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) composition keeps scenes self-contained and reusable — each component has one job, (2) deep inheritance creates tight coupling and fragile base classes, (3) Has-A (child nodes with behavior) is more flexible than Is-A (inheriting from a Damageable class). Key insight: a character doesn't inherit from Damageable, it HAS a Health component as a child.

prompt: Explain the 'signal up, call down' rule and why it matters for scene reusability.
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) children emit signals to notify (observer pattern — doesn't know who listens), (2) parents call methods on children directly ($Child.method()), (3) siblings never talk directly — ancestor mediates. Why: this keeps scenes self-contained. A Health node can be used in any game because it doesn't reference specific other nodes — it just signals.

prompt: You're designing a chest that opens when the player approaches. What nodes would you compose and how would it communicate?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) Area2D to detect player proximity, (2) Sprite2D for visuals, (3) AnimationPlayer for open animation, (4) emits an 'opened' signal — the level/spawner listens. The chest doesn't spawn loot itself. Key insight: the chest is self-contained because it signals what happened rather than directly manipulating other objects.

prompt: What would happen if you put movement code using move_and_slide() in _process() instead of _physics_process()?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) _process runs at variable rate tied to framerate — movement becomes inconsistent across machines, (2) _physics_process runs at fixed rate (60/s) regardless of rendering speed, (3) collision detection expects consistent timing — variable-rate can cause tunneling through walls on lag spikes. Key: anything with move_and_slide() belongs in _physics_process.

prompt: Why should you use @onready for node references instead of assigning them at the top of the script?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) at parse time the node tree doesn't exist yet — $Path would fail, (2) @onready defers initialization until _ready() when all children are in the tree, (3) it's equivalent to assigning in _ready() but more concise and keeps declarations together at the top of the file.

prompt: When would you use @export vs a regular variable? Give an example of each.
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) @export exposes the variable in the Inspector — use for values designers should tweak without code (speed, health, scene references), (2) regular variables are internal state the editor shouldn't see (current velocity, state machine state). Example: @export var speed: float = 200.0 (tunable), var current_direction := Vector2.ZERO (internal).

prompt: Name the 3 main lifecycle callbacks, when each runs, and what kind of logic belongs in each.
expected_answer: (1) _ready(): once when node enters tree — init, references, signal connections. (2) _process(delta): every rendered frame — visuals, UI, non-physics input. (3) _physics_process(delta): fixed tick (60/s) — movement, collision, raycasts. Key: always multiply movement by delta for framerate independence.

prompt: Order these from most general to most specific in Godot's class hierarchy:
Match each GDScript keyword to its purpose:
pairs: Initialize variable after node enters tree
Declare a custom event other nodes can listen to
Expose variable in the Inspector panel
